evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.1: prīma illa puerīlī īnstitūtiōne
terms.comment: Teaching and training at any age: Quintilian’s Īnstitūtiō ōrātōria is the orator’s education. To educate is īnstituere or ērudīre; educated, ērudītus; uneducated, inērudītus or indoctus (Traupman 29, 152, 158, 308, 400).

terms.gloss: upbringing; the education of a child
evidence: Cic. de Or. 3.125: īnstitūtus līberāliter ēducātiōne doctrīnāque puerīlī
terms.comment: The bringing-up of a child, at home and at school: Quintilian’s old man counts what he paid the music and geometry teachers among the costs of the boy’s ēducātiō (1.10.18). Strictly it is rearing, of children and of animals (Traupman 29): ēdūcit obstetrīx, ēducat nūtrīx, īnstituit paedagōgus, docet magister (Varro ap. Non. 447, Lewis & Short s.v. ēducō).

terms.gloss: teaching, training; a system of education
terms.comment: Disciplīna puerīlis is Cicero’s phrase for the schooling of freeborn children, which the Romans, unlike the Greeks, never fixed by law (Rep. 4.3).

terms.gloss: instruction; learning, the education a person has
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.1: omnis ērudītiōnis expertem
terms.comment: Far more often the learning that instruction leaves than the instruction itself (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Cicerō noster dum ego absum nōn cessāvit apud rhētorem. dē ejus ērudītiōne quod labōrēs nihil est, quoniam ingenium ejus nōstī, studium ego videō.
phrases.english: Our Cicero has not been idle at his rhetoric teacher’s while I’ve been away. As for his education, there is nothing for you to worry about: his ability you know, and his application I can see.

phrases.latin: Magna nōbīs puerīs, Quīnte frāter, sī memoriā tenēs, opīniō fuit L. Crassum nōn plūs attigisse doctrīnae quam quantum prīma illa puerīlī īnstitūtiōne potuisset; M. autem Antōnium omnīnō omnis ērudītiōnis expertem atque ignārum fuisse
phrases.english: When we were boys, brother Quintus, if you remember, it was widely believed that Lucius Crassus had acquired no more learning than his first schooling could give him, and that Marcus Antonius had had no education at all

phrases.latin: ut ager quamvīs fertilis sine cultūrā frūctuōsus esse nōn potest, sīc sine doctrīnā animus
phrases.english: as a field, however fertile, cannot bear fruit without cultivation, so a mind cannot without education
